newsitem.title: USA: New rules will free good land, keep CRP large-USDA.
newsitem.headline: New rules will free good land, keep CRP large-USDA.

text.p: The Conservation Reserve -- the biggest land retirement program in U.S. history -- will be retooled to keep top-quality farmland in crop production while sheltering fragile land from erosion, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Wednesday.
During a news conference, Glickman described the change in focus, mandated by Congress in the "Freedom to Farm" law, as "a major shift in farmland conservation policies."
"Gone will be the days of retiring productive farmland" as a way to boost farmer income or limit crop output, he said.

USDA intends to hold its first signup under a new set of operating rules for the Conservation Reserve early next year. The new rules were unveiled at the news conference. A 45-day period was set for comment before a permanent version would be issued.
Overall, land would need an erodibility index of eight or higher to qualify for enrollment. At a signup, farmers offer land and specify the rental rate they want. USDA decides which bids to accept.
Size of the Conservation Reserve was not expected to shrink dramatically, Glickman said.
"It's not my desire to be stingy," Glickman said.

About 108 million acres of U.S. farmland potentially could be offered for the reserve, which is limited to 36.4 million acres. Created in 1985, the program pays farmers an annual rent for idling fragile land for 10 years.

While emphasizing the goal of soil and water conservation, Glickman said attention also was given to "the great needs for American food production." U.S. grain and oilseed supplies were forecast to remain tight through 1997.
But, Glickman refused to suggest what farmers should do, either expanding crop acreage or putting land in the reserve.
"Those decisions will be made by the farmers," Glickman said, adding that the "Freedom to Farm" law had ended most of the government's power to control crop acreage.

The Coalition for a Competitive Food and Agricultural System, an umbrella group for exporters, farm suppliers and food processors, said too much high-quality land with no erosion potential was tied up in the reserve and should be returned to use. It also said USDA rents were too high.
Under USDA's proposed rules, rent would be based on local cash rentals with adjustments for each parcel. Water purity, soil erosion and wildlife habitat would be major goals.
